summary:
Martian-Map is a 3D, browser-based globe of Mars that lets anyone fly from orbit down to a 3 × 3 km site inside Gale crater and plan a walk across it. We call that walk Marswalk.

The globe combines official NASA and USGS data:
 Global surface: the Viking MDIM 2.1 colorized mosaic over the MOLA–HRSC elevation model.
 Landing site: 1 m terrain and 25 cm imagery of the boxwork ridges of Mount Sharp, plus a slope map and THEMIS night-time thermal data.

On top of that terrain we traced a real route: the path the Curiosity rover drove through the boxwork between sols 4530 and 4720. It has five scientific stops, each with its objective, its hazards and real rover photos. The app computes the route's elevation profile, distance, climb, maximum slope and walking time. It also flags dangerous slopes in green, yellow and red.
details:
Martian-Map is an interactive 3D Mars you can open in a web browser. You can spin the whole planet, read coordinates and elevation under the cursor, and fly to 12 named landmarks from the IAU Gazetteer of Planetary Nomenclature, such as Olympus Mons, Hellas and Gale crater. You can also move the Sun to see relief cast shadows, and exaggerate the terrain vertically to make subtle landforms visible.

When you fly into Gale crater, the map switches to the highest-resolution data available for the boxwork region of Mount Sharp: a 1 m terrain model, 25 cm orthoimagery, a slope layer (green below 10°, yellow from 10° to 20°, red above 20°) and a THEMIS night-time infrared layer, where warm areas tend to be rock and cool areas sand.

The route follows the real traverse of the Curiosity rover: about 1.24 km, with 80 m of climb and 29 m of descent. Its five waypoints sit at actual rover stops. Each one shows its science objective, its hazards (narrow ridges, loose sand, steep slopes), a planned stop time and photos taken by Curiosity at that place. A live elevation profile gives distance, climb, maximum slope and estimated walking time.

Under the hood, a Python pipeline cuts the raw scientific rasters (GeoTIFFs) into map tiles: imagery tiles for the global mosaic and each site layer, and 3D terrain tiles in the quantized-mesh format with lighting normals. All tiles are computed on the true IAU Mars ellipsoid (3396.19 by 3376.20 km), not on Earth's, and the browser renders them with CesiumJS.

What benefits does it have?

Real data, measured accuracy: we checked the app against the source data. Olympus Mons reads +21,093 m in the app against +21,121 m in the elevation model, and Hellas reads -7,425 m against -7,468 m. The route and waypoints are real Curiosity positions.

Planning, not just viewing: slope classes, hazards and walking time turn imagery into an actual traverse plan.

Works offline: the app makes zero requests to external servers, so it can run in a classroom, a museum or a field setting without internet.

Reproducible: every tile is generated by documented, containerized scripts, so anyone can rebuild the map from the public source datasets.

What is the intended impact?

We want people to experience Mars as a place you could walk on, not just a picture. Students and the public can follow a real rover traverse and understand why scientists chose each stop. Mission planners and educators get a lightweight template: any landing site with a terrain model and imagery can be plugged into the same pipeline and become a walkable, annotated route.

What tools, languages, hardware or software did we use?

Frontend: TypeScript, Svelte 5 and SvelteKit, Vite, and CesiumJS 1.147 for the 3D globe and terrain rendering.

Data pipeline: Python 3.13 with NumPy, Rasterio, Pillow and quantized-mesh-encoder, running in a Podman container for reproducibility.

GIS: GDAL for reprojection, resampling, slope computation and inspection, and QGIS for site selection, slope review and route tracing.

Data: for the global surface, the MGS MOLA - MEX HRSC Blended DEM (NASA/JPL/GSFC, ESA/DLR/FU Berlin, USGS) and the Viking MDIM 2.1 colorized mosaic (NASA/JPL, USGS). For the site, the MSL Gale merged 1 m DEM and 25 cm orthophoto, derived from HiRISE (NASA/JPL/University of Arizona, USGS). For thermal data, Mars Odyssey THEMIS IR Night 100 m (NASA/JPL/ASU). For the rover, the Curiosity traverse and waypoints from NASA's MMGIS "Where is Curiosity?" map, plus raw Curiosity images. For place names, the IAU/USGS Gazetteer of Planetary Nomenclature.

Collaboration: Git and GitHub, with a written interface contract between team members and handoff notes between shifts.

Hardware: our personal laptops. No special hardware is needed to run the app; any computer with a modern web browser works.

How is our project creative?

It follows a real rover. Instead of an invented path, Marswalk follows Curiosity's real drive through the boxwork. That gives every stop real science and real photos, and it shows the route can actually be driven.

It is built for Mars. Most web map tools quietly assume Earth. We rebuilt the globe, the terrain tiles and every coordinate convention for Mars: the IAU ellipsoid, planetocentric latitude, east-positive longitude and heights above the MOLA areoid. That keeps the data aligned to the meter.

It turns layers into a story. Slope, thermal data, imagery and terrain are combined into one question: "Can I walk here, and why would I want to?" The answer appears as color, a profile and a time estimate.

It is honest about danger. One waypoint is on purpose a lookout above 20° of slope, so the map's warning shows up during the demo.
